Rothschilds & Money Schemes

One family, five banking houses, and the money of a continent. This page follows the Rothschilds from Frankfurt’s Judengasse to the capitals of Europe — how their houses in Frankfurt, London, Paris, Vienna and Naples came to stand behind the loans, the railways, the gold and the silver of the nineteenth century — and sets beside them the other Jewish banking figures of the age. The material is arranged in date order, and where two threads meet at the same turning point, each points to the other.

20 album items · documents and sources throughout

The companion investigation: The Greenbacks — the 1878 “slaves to gold” article and the policy behind it

The Rothschilds — Frankfurt, and the five sons

The name comes from a house sign. In Frankfurt’s Judengasse — the street where the city’s Jews were required to live — houses were known not by numbers but by the signs they carried, and the family’s house carried a red shield: zum Rothen Schild, “at the red shield.” The house itself had been built in 1567 by Isaak Elchanan Bacharach, whose family tree is set out in the documents below. A red shield still stands at the centre of the family’s coat of arms.

Mayer Amschel Rothschild (born Frankfurt, February 23, 1744; died Frankfurt, September 19, 1812) was the son of Amschel Moses Rothschild, a money changer who had traded with the Prince of Hesse. Mayer Amschel became a court factor — a financial agent — to the Landgraves of Hesse-Kassel, and from the 1760s built a banking business out of the coin and antiquities trade. When Napoleon’s armies invaded Hesse in 1806, the Elector William I entrusted his fortune to Mayer Amschel, who kept it through the occupation and returned it — the episode painted by Moritz Daniel Oppenheim below.

What Mayer Amschel did that earlier court factors had not was to send his five sons out to five capitals and keep the five houses one family firm:

  • Amschel Mayer (1773–1855) — Frankfurt, the mother house.
  • Salomon Mayer (1774–1855) — Vienna.
  • Nathan Mayer (1777–1836) — London.
  • Carl Mayer (1788–1855) — Naples.
  • James Mayer (1792–1868) — Paris.

The coat of arms the brothers received when the Austrian Emperor Francis I made all five of them barons (Freiherr) on September 29, 1822, carries a fist holding five arrows — one for each son’s house. Between the 1820s and the 1870s the five houses together dominated international finance in Europe. Each house is taken up in its own country section below, in the order Germany, Britain, France, Austria, Italy.

Sources: Rothschild family — reference article · The Rothschild Archive — timeline · The Bacharach family tree (document)

Monetary systems by country

Germany — the Frankfurt house

The Frankfurt house, M. A. Rothschild & Söhne, stayed in the Judengasse where the family began, under the eldest son, Amschel Mayer. From Frankfurt the family financed some of the earliest German railways: the terminus of the Taunus railway, opened in 1840 and one of Germany’s first lines, was Rothschild-financed. The family’s first great state loan — £5 million to Prussia in 1818 — was arranged by Nathan from London (see Britain).

Berlin, the rising Prussian capital, had no Rothschild house of its own. The Rothschilds’ Berlin business ran through the bank of S. Bleichröder, which acted as their branch office in the city; and when Bismarck, leaving Frankfurt in 1858, asked Baron Mayer Carl von Rothschild to name him a Berlin banker, the name the Rothschilds gave him was Gerson Bleichröder — who became Bismarck’s private banker and the financial hand of German unification (see Other Jewish banking figures). The Frankfurt mother house itself closed in 1901, the last of the five but two to go.

Sources: Rothschild family — reference article · The Rothschild Archive — timeline · Gerson von Bleichröder — reference article

Britain — Nathan in London

Nathan Mayer Rothschild began in Manchester in 1806 in the textile trade, moved to London, took the premises at 2 New Court, St Swithin’s Lane, in 1809, and established N. M. Rothschild & Sons in 1811. From London he organised the money of the war against Napoleon: in 1813–1815 the shipment and transfer of bullion to Wellington’s armies and the payment of Britain’s subsidies to its allies — £9.8 million in subsidy loans in 1815 alone. The gold side of that work is told in Gold. In 1818 he arranged the £5 million loan to Prussia. By 1825–26 he was able to supply enough coin to the Bank of England to enable it to avert a market liquidity crisis — Wellington’s verdict was that without “the most extraordinary exertions — above all on the part of old Rothschild — the Bank must have stopped payment.”

Nathan’s brother-in-law Moses Montefiore, whose firm acted as stockbrokers to Nathan, is in Other Jewish banking figures. The album holds a Spanish newspaper page on a later London Rothschild — item M382, on Alfredo (Alfred) de Rothschild, whom “all the cabmen and omnibus drivers of London know” — and a book page, item M355, telling the Waterloo stock-exchange story as legend had it: that Nathan, secretly worded that Wellington and Blücher had failed to join, let English funds fall and bought through agents, clearing five million dollars. The documented record runs the other way — the family took the Waterloo news straight to the government, and the advance-news killing is a fiction repeated in later popular accounts; the Rothschilds’ real Waterloo business was the gold commission told in Gold.

Sources: Rothschild family — reference article · The Rothschild Archive — Rothschild and gold

France — James in Paris

James Mayer de Rothschild was in Paris from 1811–12, aged nineteen, co-ordinating the purchase of specie and bullion for his brother Nathan; in 1814–15 he was the linchpin of Nathan’s plan to supply Wellington’s armies with funds. In 1817 the firm took the name de Rothschild Frères, with his brothers as partners, and became the French government’s banker through the Restoration and the July Monarchy. In 1832 James became the official papal banker (see Italy). In 1845 the French government awarded him the contract for the Chemin de Fer du Nord, France’s first major railway, running from Paris toward Valenciennes and designed to join the Austrian lines built by his brother Salomon; James was the Nord company’s president from its founding until his death in 1868.

Sources: The Rothschild Archive — timeline · Chemins de fer du Nord — reference article · Rothschild loans to the Holy See — reference article

Austria — Salomon in Vienna, and the Creditanstalt

Salomon Mayer von Rothschild established the Vienna bank in 1820 and became the Habsburg monarchy’s financier: a confidant of Chancellor Prince Metternich, a discreet lender to the Bohemian and Hungarian nobility, and the financier of the Emperor Ferdinand Northern Railway in the 1830s. His son Anselm Salomon von Rothschild (1803–1874) founded, in 1855, the k.k. privilegierte Österreichische Credit-Anstalt für Handel und Gewerbe — the Creditanstalt — which grew into the largest bank of the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy and was led by members of the Rothschild family until 1931.

Sources: Anselm Salomon von Rothschild — reference article · Creditanstalt — reference article

Italy — Carl in Naples, and the Pope’s loans

Carl Mayer von Rothschild founded C. M. de Rothschild & Figli in Naples. His bank arranged substantial loans to the Papal States and to the kings of Naples, the Duchy of Parma and the Grand Duchy of Tuscany. The famous transaction came in 1832: with the Papal States’ finances in disorder after the Napoleonic wars, an agreement signed on November 30, 1831, brought a Rothschild loan of £400,000 to the Holy See into force under Pope Gregory XVI. Carl travelled to Rome in January 1832 to meet the Pope — and, observers noted, was not required to kiss the Pope’s feet, as other visitors were. His brother James became the official papal banker, and the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 described the Rothschilds as “the guardians of the papal treasure.” The Naples house closed in 1863, after Italian unification swept away the courts it had served.

Sources: Rothschild loans to the Holy See — reference article · Rothschild family — reference article

Silver

Until 1873 the United States coined both gold and silver. The Coinage Act of February 12, 1873, ended the standard silver dollar — silver was demonetized — and the silver states and the debtor farmers spent the next quarter-century fighting to undo it. The album’s newspaper pages carry the fight in its own words:

  • Item M011 — a “SILVER DEMONETIZED” page naming the coinage law of February 12, 1873, and the More Money League of America of Fitzgerald, Georgia.
  • Item M012 — the Silver City front page above, from the height of the 1896 free-silver campaign.
  • Item M010 — the silver debate in Congress: “Will he Buy Coined Silver at $1.32 and Sell it to us for $1.29?” — “Do you want to make the United States the dumping ground for all the silver of the world?”

Five years after demonetization, Congress partly reversed course: the Bland-Allison Act of February 28, 1878, passed over President Hayes’s veto, ordered the Treasury to buy and coin two to four million dollars’ worth of silver every month. Five weeks later, on April 4, 1878, the Saint Paul Anti-Monopolist printed the article at the centre of the companion investigation, The Greenbacks, where the whole policy record — resumption, the silver acts, the court fights — is set out. In 1890 the Sherman Silver Purchase Act obliged the Treasury to buy still more silver; in 1893, with gold draining out of the Treasury, the purchase clause was repealed — and the drain ran straight into the gold crisis of 1895 told in Gold.

Silver’s enemies, in the period’s own verse, had a name. The album preserves a newspaper poem in the Rothschilds’ supposed voice — items M044–M047 — beginning “Hater of silver / And all around / Manipulator / Of / Finances. / I own the world! / Its people are my / Slaves…”

Cross-reference: silver demonetized in 1873 is the hinge of this page’s timeline — it is where the money of the United States, and then of Europe, swung onto gold alone. See Gold.

Sources: The Eagle (Silver City, N.M.), Sept. 30, 1896 — Library of Congress · The Greenbacks — the policy record · Reuters — the history of financing America (1895 episode)

Gold

1809. Nathan Rothschild conducted his first recorded deal in gold bullion in London, and soon held a leading position as a bullion broker in the City.

1814–1815 — the Waterloo commission. Wellington’s armies in Spain and France had to be paid in coin that could be spent where they stood. In January 1814 the Commissary-in-Chief, J. C. Herries, formally engaged Nathan to supply it. Nathan instructed his brothers on the continent to buy gold wherever they could, secretly and in small quantities so as not to disturb the market; the gold was shipped and conveyed to Wellington in southern France. In 1815 the need arose again, and the money raised by the Rothschilds paid the 209,000 English, Dutch and Prussian soldiers assembled in Belgium before Waterloo. Nathan called it “the best business I ever did.” (The stock-exchange legend that later grew over Waterloo is dealt with in Britain.)

1825. In the crash of 1825 the Bank of England ran desperately short of coined gold; the Rothschilds supplied a large volume of gold and averted a suspension of payment.

1852. N. M. Rothschild & Sons took on the Royal Mint Refinery in London — a lease the firm would hold for over a hundred years.

1873. With silver demonetized (see Silver), gold stood alone as the standard metal of the money systems — the position the Saint Paul article of 1878 protested in the words “To be slaves to gold is to be slaves to the Rothchilds and German Jews” (see The Greenbacks).

1895 — the American gold rescue. Silver purchases and gold exports had driven the United States Treasury’s gold reserve down toward $41 million. On February 8, 1895, the Treasury signed a contract with a syndicate: the contract, printed by Congress, names “August Belmont and Company, of New York, on behalf of Messrs. N. M. Rothschild and Sons, of London, England, and themselves, and Messrs. J. P. Morgan and Company, of New York.” The syndicate sold the United States 3,500,000 ounces of gold coin — at least half of it to be obtained in Europe — for some $62 million in 4 per cent thirty-year bonds, and the reserve was restored above $100 million. The younger August Belmont who sat with Morgan and President Cleveland is in Other Jewish banking figures.

1919–2004 — the gold fixing. On September 12, 1919, the five principal London bullion firms — N. M. Rothschild & Sons, Mocatta & Goldsmid, Pixley & Abell, Samuel Montagu & Co., and Sharps Wilkins — performed the first London gold fixing, setting the price at £4 18s 9d per troy ounce. For more than eighty years the fixing met at Rothschild’s New Court offices, with Rothschild in the chair; it was suspended while the London gold market was closed, 1939–1954. In April 2004 N. M. Rothschild & Sons withdrew from gold trading and from the fixing, and the chairmanship it had held permanently began to rotate.

Sources: The Rothschild Archive — Rothschild and gold · The Rothschild Archive — the gold fixing room, New Court · Gold fixing — reference article · Morgan–Belmont Agreement — encyclopedia entry · The 1895 contract — House report, 53rd Congress (PDF) · Rothschild & Co — interviews on gold (PDF)

Other Jewish banking figures

The Rothschilds were the head of the group, not the whole of it. The Jewish Encyclopedia wrote in 1906 that the practice the Rothschilds began — brothers of one firm planted in the different financial centres — “was followed by other Jewish financiers, like the Bischoffsheims, Pereires, Seligmans, Lazards and others,” and that by this means Jewish financiers obtained an increasing share of international finance. The figures below are the ones this collection’s record touches, in birth order.

Moses Montefiore (1784–1885)

Born at Livorno in 1784 to a London Sephardic family, Montefiore bought one of the twelve brokers’ licences then open to Jews on the London Stock Exchange, made his fortune rapidly, and retired from business in 1824. His marriage to Judith Cohen made him brother-in-law to Nathan Rothschild, for whom Montefiore’s firm acted as stockbrokers and underwrote the loans Rothschild floated. He helped found the Alliance Assurance Company, the Imperial Continental Gas Association and the Provincial Bank of Ireland; in 1837 he was elected sheriff of London and knighted, and in 1846 made a baronet. The fortune made in the City funded the second career for which he is remembered — sixty years of travel and intercession on behalf of Jews abroad.

Sources: Sir Moses Montefiore — Britannica · Montefiore — Dictionary of National Biography (Wikisource)

August Belmont, father and son (1813–1890; 1853–1924)

August Belmont & Co. of New York was the Rothschilds’ American house — August Belmont the elder came to New York as the family’s agent and built the firm that bore his name. It is the younger Belmont, his son, who appears in the record here: in February 1895 he and J. P. Morgan led the syndicate that sold gold to the United States Treasury, Belmont’s firm acting, in the contract’s words, “on behalf of Messrs. N. M. Rothschild and Sons, of London.” The full transaction is told in Gold.

Sources: Morgan–Belmont Agreement — encyclopedia entry · The 1895 contract — House report, 53rd Congress (PDF)

Gerson von Bleichröder (1822–1893)

The Berlin banker of the unification era. His father Samuel founded the firm of S. Bleichröder in Berlin in 1803; the house acted as the Rothschilds’ branch office in Berlin, where the family kept no house of their own. In 1858, on the recommendation of Baron Mayer Carl von Rothschild, Bleichröder took over Bismarck’s private banking and the placing of loans for the Prussian state — work that continued for the German Empire after 1871 and put him at the financial centre of unification (see Germany). After the Franco-Prussian War he was summoned to Versailles as financial adviser on the French war indemnity, and received the Iron Cross; in 1872 he was raised to the hereditary nobility — one of the first Jews in Prussia so honoured without conversion.

Sources: Gerson von Bleichröder — reference article

Jacob Schiff (1847–1920)

Schiff was born in Frankfurt’s Judengasse in 1847; his father Moses was a broker for the Rothschilds. He emigrated to New York, married Therese Loeb, and from 1885 headed the banking house of Kuhn, Loeb & Co., which under him became one of the two most powerful private investment banks in the United States, financing the railroads’ expansion. His most famous transaction came in the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–05: Kuhn, Loeb floated $200 million in loans for Japan — the first major Japanese bond issue on Wall Street, providing roughly half the funds Japan needed for the war. Schiff, angered by the Tsarist regime’s treatment of the Jews, consistently refused to take part in loans for Russia and used his influence to keep other firms from underwriting them.

Sources: Schiff, Jacob Henry — Encyclopaedia Judaica entry · Jacob Schiff — reference article: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Schiff

Paul Warburg (1868–1932)

Warburg came from the Hamburg banking house of M. M. Warburg & Co., founded by his great-grandfather in 1798. He married Nina Loeb and in 1902 settled in New York as a partner in Kuhn, Loeb & Co., under Jacob Schiff. Appalled at the primitive state of American banking, he campaigned in speeches and essays for a central reserve institution; his plan, taken up by Senator Aldrich’s committee, reached its final, modified form in the Federal Reserve Act of 1913, and President Wilson appointed him to the first Federal Reserve Board, where he served 1914–1918. The album holds the other side of his fame: item M061, a page of the Dearborn Independent headlined with “the Remarkable Story of Paul Warburg, Who Began Work on the Monetary System After Three Weeks’ Residence.” Father Coughlin’s Social Justice, in the documents below, likewise put Warburg’s influence on the Federal Reserve’s final form on a par with its sponsor Carter Glass’s.

Sources: Paul Moritz Warburg — encyclopedia entry · Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis — Warburg’s crusade for a central bank

Baron Maurice de Hirsch (1831–1896)

The richest of them all has his own page in this collection: Baron Hirsch & the Colonies — the railway fortune, the Jewish Colonization Association, and the farm colonies of Argentina and America. The album’s money pages touch him twice more: item M235 prints a London rumour that the Rothschilds would issue a $200,000,000 Russian loan, alongside the report that Hirsch’s widow had given £4,000,000 to promote the emigration of Russian Jews to Argentina.

Sources: Baron Hirsch & the Colonies — this collection

The Greenbacks — the companion investigation

The American paper-money fight has its own featured page: The Greenbacks — the April 4, 1878, Anti-Monopolist article “THE NEW DEPARTURE,” printed in full exactly as it appeared (“To be slaves to gold is to be slaves to the Rothchilds and German Jews”), the original page at the Library of Congress, and the policy record behind the greenback from the Legal Tender Act of 1862 to resumption in 1879. Two documents on this page’s shelf belong with it: the Hazard Circular of July 1862 — “capital shall control labor by controlling wages… It will not do to allow the greenback, as it is called, to circulate as money any length of time, as we cannot control that” — and the album’s book page item M071, on the white planters of the South as “the slaves of the Jews, who control the money market.”
